The following extract is from a letter written by Daniel Coker, to his wife in this CITY. We have obtained permission to publish it, in the expectation that it will be found interesting to many our readers.

Genoy, Africa, Mar. 19, 1820. When the ship Elizabeth returned, I wrote to you and many others, and sent my Journal but not knowing whether that ship arrived safe or not and as I have, of necessity, to write to the Colonization Society, and at the same time a way of conveyance, send you this letter—we had short passage to Africa. I performed you one of my letters by the Elizabeth, as above mentioned, and one in hand you from Sierra Leone; our passage was 30 days. We had a kind reception among the natives as could have been expected.—All our people were favored with good health while crossing the sea, except what is called the sea sickness; but, unfortunately for us, we landed in one of the most unhealthy spots perhaps, on the coast, a small island of Mr. Jones. It is very low and sometimes overflows—is covered with mangroves, and the water is very bad; but he had prepared some shacks, and gave us the offer of occupying them until we got our land which we bought in a few weeks time—so we highly received the offer, which we since have had cause to regret. We had not long been there—and in a few weeks after the Elizabeth sailed, the most of our people were taken down with fever; among the rest. Mr. Crozar, the agent of the Colonial Society, soon departed this life; a few days before he died, he transferred his office to me without my knowledge. When Mr. Bacon brought the appointment to me—I refused to accept it, but the other agent of the States, said, if refused, the whole business would most likely fall through—and I must go immediately to attend the palaver at the town of King Sherbro, 10 miles off called Ionee. I went and have been better than four weeks in Palaver, and have not been back since, nor could not. I was so busily engaged. Since left there Mr. Bacon has died, and Mr. Branson died last Saturday. All three of the agents that came are no more, and two persons of color also. Learning that Mr. Peck was very ill, I sent for him to come to me at Ionee, he came and has got quite well and hearty. I received a letter yesterday from the Governor of Sierra Leone, to remove my people to Cape Shilling, or Sierra Leone, but the reason I did not comply, is, that I am to go to morrow to the Baloo, the place we expect to get; it has good water and is high and healthy, and I shall try to set houses and remove our people to their own place immediately. Our people are now all including, for they have water there. As to what I have passed through, my Journal must tell. I will keep on writing until you come, which I hope will be shortly, and thousands of others will. It could not but be expected that the first emigrants would suffer very much; I calculated it, but those who come after, will find it smooth and pleasant—I shall do all in my power to make things as comfortable as possible for your reception, and all in my power for the general good. Should my life be spared, I will that Nicholas and Deayer here now, but it is in vain to wish; tell every body that can do good to this people to come as soon as possible, for here they may be happy.—Bring everything you can, for nothing that you want in America will be useless here, either to wear, to eat, or as furniture—tell the people that come the same. Those who wish to trade bring tobacco, calico, iron pots, knives and forks, spoons, handkerchiefs, needles and awls, all pipes.—You can buy fowl for two pipes and large one for three pipes; bring shoes and what else they think proper. I have written to the Secretary of the Society for my passage. Oh that God may bless you and send you here in peace. Give my love to all the dear friends, and to you and relations. I would say more, but H. Shin is about starting for England, and I have to meet the Kings this morning; I am full of business. I was sent the other day by the kings to see our land, and am much pleased; it is good, fertile and healthy, and plenty of most excellent water. The Kings go to day to give me leave to go for the Colonization Society. Mr. Pei gives much love to you and his family. He is well. Africa is good land; tell the people to come here and they will be happy. It will be industrious. DANIEL COKER.
